question: What is the meaning of potential for reuse in relation to end-of-life management?
description: The potential for reuse in relation to end-of-life management refers to the possibility of effectively reusing products or their components after their initial use, thereby reducing waste and conserving resources. This concept is central to identifying products where reuse would result in environmental benefits, as highlighted in the provided text. The significance of reuse potential assessment lies in guiding the selection of products for reuse to ensure economic viability and sustainability, as well as in facilitating environmental impact assessments for reuse. This approach emphasizes the feasibility of reuse and supports circular economy strategies by promoting the reuse of materials embedded in buildings, thereby reducing the consumption of virgin materials and minimizing waste.

A B S T R A C T   
Concerns about the increasing global consumption of non-renewable resources as well as shortages of primary 
raw materials and reduction of space available for final disposal of waste are raising important issues for the 
society. Additionally, the unsustainable treatment of resources belongs to the main concerns of the EU, resulting 
in the development of strategies for maximizing recycling rates in order to minimize environmental impacts and 
energy consumption caused by extraction of primary materials. 
In this paper, the Material Passport (MP) method, which evaluates the recycling potential and environmental 
impact of materials embedded in buildings, is demonstrated on a use case - a demolition object, in order to test its 
applicability at the end-of-life stage as well as to assess the recycling potential of the existing building. 
Three acquisition methods were applied on the use case in order to obtain information on the material 
composition as well as geometrical information: laser scanning, demolition acquisition (DA) and Urban Mining 
assessment (UMA), with regards to the quality and separability of the materials. A BIM-Model (Building Infor­
mation Modelling) was generated, integrating the acquired data, as well as serving as knowledge database, from 
which element lists with incorporated materials were exported and mapped to the regarding recycling grade. 
As a result, an MP is generated for the exterior walls and the foundation, delivering information on the total 
masses, the share of recycling and waste masses, as well as the environmental impacts. The recycling potential of 
the exterior walls is ~52%, whereby the foundation has a recycling potential of ~20%. The existence of an MP at 
the end-of-life stage of a building can be seen as an outstanding advantage regarding recycling and reuse, thus 
supporting circularity and sustainability in the construction sector.   
1. Introduction 
According to the WWF’s (World Wildlife Fund) living planet report, 
more than the equivalent of two planet Earth’s resources will be needed 
to meet humans’ demands of natural resources by 2030 (McLellan et al., 
2012). The construction sector is the world’s largest consumer of raw 
materials and accounts for 25–40% of global carbon emissions (WEF, 
2016 a). Moreover, this sector is also causing 25% of the total solid waste 
generated worldwide (Yeheyis et al., 2013). The mentioned facts are 
underlining the urgent need for improvement of the habits in the con­
struction industry. Thus, it is of utmost importance to reduce the con­
sumption of virgin materials and increase the reuse and recycling of 
materials in existing buildings, which can serve as secondary raw 
materials. The European Union (EU) describes secondary raw materials 
as “waste that can be recycled is injected back into the economy as 
secondary raw materials” (Eurpoean Commison, 2021). In the existing 
building stock, a large amount of materials is incorporated, which might 
be valuable materials for reuse or recycling. However, these materials 
mostly lead to waste at the end of their life-cycle. In Austria, the amount 
of secondary raw materials is even larger than the primary resources for 
many materials. Since Austria is a country that strongly depends on 
imports, reuse or recycling of materials embedded in buildings would 
reduce the dependency on imports. In many European countries, the 
situation is similar: due to a low amount of primary resources, an import 
of raw materials is necessary (Brunner and Rechberger, 2016).
